name: Kasner Anisotropic Vacuum Cosmology
description: An anisotropic vacuum cosmology that expands along some axes while contracting along another, with expansion exponents constrained by two algebraic relations. It is a key building block of the chaotic approach to cosmological singularities.
history: 1921 was the year Edward Kasner, a geometer at Columbia with no particular interest in the universe, wrote down the standard picture of its first instant. What he wanted from Einstein's field equations was a question of shape: how many flat dimensions does it take to hold a solution inside one as a curved slice? That April he proved that five will not do [kasner1921flat]. Six months later came the five page paper relativists still cite [kasner1921]. Its third section opens with the words "A simple example" and then gives, in a few lines, the metric that now carries his name: three spatial directions going as powers of the time, their exponents obeying two conditions, that they sum to one and that their squares sum to one. What the section is for is the theorem closing it: solutions of this type embed in a flat space of seven dimensions. Of the metric itself Kasner remarks only that it "can be put in the static form," which tells you what he thought he had.¶Those two conditions are a plane and a sphere. The plane $p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 1$ cuts the unit sphere $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1$ in a circle, and every Kasner universe is one point on it. Apart from three isolated points where the geometry is secretly flat, one exponent comes out negative: two axes stretch, the third squeezes, and the squeeze is compulsory. Run it back toward $t = 0$ and the stretching directions crush to nothing while the contracting one runs away, so the singularity is met not as a point but as a cigar, unboundedly long and unboundedly thin.¶In 1963 Evgeny Lifshitz and Isaak Khalatnikov took Kasner's exponents as the leading behavior of a region collapsing toward a singularity, then counted the arbitrary functions such a solution can carry, and came up short. A singularity, they concluded, is what special initial data buys you, an artifact of Friedmann's perfect symmetry rather than a verdict of the theory [lifshitz1963]. In 1965 Roger Penrose took that premise apart by assuming no symmetry whatever: once a trapped surface forms, geodesics end, and generality is no protection [penrose1965]. The Soviet position held anyway for five more years.¶What the losing side did next is the part worth telling. Hunting their own error, Lifshitz and Khalatnikov, joined by Vladimir Belinskii, found in 1970 the regime they had skipped [khalatnikov1970]. Near a singularity neighboring points stop speaking to one another, and each one alone sits in a Kasner solution for a while, hands the negative exponent to a different axis, then sits in another. The axis collapsing this epoch is expanding the next. Charles Misner had met the same oscillation in 1969 in the closed Bianchi type IX model [misner1969].¶The order in which the axes take their turn is the surprise.¶Parametrize the exponents by $u$, and each bounce sends $u$ to $u - 1$ until it falls below one, whereupon the era closes and the next opens at $1/u$, which is the map that manufactures continued fractions [bkl1970]. An irrational starting value never repeats, so the descent is chaotic. That is what the simple example of section three became: the local building block every modern account of a generic singularity is assembled from, one Kasner solution per point of space, swapped for another over and over on the way down. Kasner thought the best thing in his paper was the metric in section four, "apparently the simplest solution of Einstein's equations which has thus far been obtained." That is not the one anybody remembers.
